result.summary: Penthesileia, queen of the Amazons, comes to Troy and is welcomed by Priam, but a deceitful dream sent by Pallas urges her to fight Achilles. She routs the Greeks until Achilles and Aias arrive, and Achilles kills her, then regrets it. Thersites mocks him and is killed, and both sides bury their dead.

scenes.title: Penthesileia arrives at Troy
scenes.summary: The frightened Trojans welcome Penthesileia, who came to Troy to cleanse the guilt of killing her sister Hippolyte. Priam feasts her and she vows to kill Achilles.
scenes.stakes: Penthesileia risks her life against Achilles; Troy risks falling.

scenes.title: Andromache's warning and the dream
scenes.summary: Andromache silently foresees Penthesileia's doom. At night Pallas sends a false dream in the shape of her father.
scenes.stakes: Penthesileia is lured by a lying dream toward death.

scenes.title: Arming and Priam's prayer
scenes.summary: Penthesileia arms and rides out with the Trojans. Priam prays to Zeus, and an eagle seizing a dove frightens him.
scenes.stakes: Priam fears losing the last hope of Troy.

scenes.title: Slaughter on the plain
scenes.summary: Trojans and Amazons fight the Greeks. Many die on both sides, and Penthesileia drives the Greeks back.
scenes.stakes: The Greek host faces rout and burning ships.

scenes.title: Trojan women stopped by Theano
scenes.summary: Tisiphone urges the women to fight, but Theano persuades them to stay home.
scenes.stakes: The women risk death in battle they are untrained for.

scenes.title: Achilles kills Penthesileia
scenes.summary: Aias and Achilles arm and rejoin the battle. Achilles pierces Penthesileia and her horse with one spear, and the Trojans flee.
scenes.stakes: Penthesileia faces death; the Greek ships face fire.

scenes.title: Achilles' remorse; Ares restrained
scenes.summary: Achilles taunts the dying queen, then is struck by her beauty and feels love. Ares rushes to avenge her but Zeus checks him with thunderbolts.
scenes.stakes: Ares risks Zeus's thunderbolt if he attacks Achilles.

scenes.title: Thersites killed
scenes.summary: Thersites mocks Achilles' pity and Achilles kills him with one blow. Diomedes, his kinsman, is angry, but the chiefs reconcile them.
scenes.stakes: Achilles and Diomedes nearly come to blows.

scenes.title: Funerals and feast
scenes.summary: The Greeks return Penthesileia's body, and the Trojans bury her with Laomedon. The Greeks bury Podarces and dishonour Thersites, then feast in Agamemnon's tent.

alias_notes.explanation: Patronymic: son of Peleus; also called son of Aeacus after his grandfather.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable statement of mercy toward dead enemies.
Tisiphone argues women share men's nature and strength.

analysis.text: Fate and divine deception drive Penthesileia to a doomed glory, and her beauty in death turns Achilles' triumph into remorse.
The poem contrasts women's roles in war and at home, as in Theano's speech sending women back to the loom.

legacy.text: Penthesileia and Achilles' love for the dying queen became a favourite subject of later art and literature, including Kleist's play Penthesilea (1808).

fun_facts.text: This poem, by Quintus of Smyrna, was written in Greek probably in the 3rd or 4th century AD as a continuation of the Iliad.

language_notes.text: Peleides means 'son of Peleus', a patronymic for Achilles. 'Ravined up' means devoured greedily; 'kine' are cattle.
'Stout-heart Aeacus' son' is another way of naming Achilles; his father Peleus was himself a son of Aeacus, so here it means grandson.
Scamander is the river of Troy; Achilles choked it with corpses. 'Brought the Trojans doom' alludes to his arrival at Troy by sea.
Thermodon is the river in northern Anatolia by the Black Sea, traditionally the homeland of the Amazons.
The Erinnyes (Furies) were avenging spirits who pursued those guilty of shedding kindred blood; 'The Awful Ones' is a respectful name for them.
'The tireless War-god's child' refers to Penthesileia as daughter of Ares, whom the Romans called Mars; 'mailed' means armoured.
A 'leech' is an old word for a physician.
"Vaunt" means a boast. The wild queen is Penthesileia, the Amazon, who has just boasted she will kill Achilles.
"Aweless" means fearless, not inspiring awe in himself; here it describes Achilles, son of Peleus, as undaunted.
"The city through" is inverted word order for "throughout the city"; the people regarded Hector as a god.
She wishes she had been buried dead before Hector was speared; "Or ever" means "before".
Refers to Achilles dragging Hector's body behind his chariot around Troy's walls after killing him.
Ocean is the great river encircling the world in Greek belief; the sun was imagined setting into it.
"Hest" is an archaic word for command.
"Trito-born" is an epithet of Pallas Athena, of uncertain origin, linked to Lake Triton or the name Triton.
"The sunless land" is the underworld, the traditional source of false dreams.
Greaves are armour plates protecting the shins; here they are gold.
"Brand" means sword; "massy" means massive or heavy.
A halberd here is a great battle-axe, "sharp of either blade" meaning double-edged.
"Theretofore" means up to that time; the champions had previously shrunk from facing Achilles.
Harpies were storm-spirits with wings, proverbial for speed. Oreithyia was an Athenian princess carried off by the North Wind (Boreas).
Tritonis is Athena, who fought beside the gods against the Giants in their war on Olympus.
"Cronos' Son" is Zeus, and "Laomedon's child" is Priam; the periphrasis names both without using their names.
"Vouchsafe" means grant graciously; "unscathed" means unharmed.
An eagle was Zeus's bird, and its omens were read; an eagle seizing a dove portends the strong destroying the weak, here to the left, an ill sign.
Argives: Greeks, named from Argos; the poem also calls them Danaans. Ares' child: Penthesileia is a daughter of the war-god Ares.
Corslets are body armour for the chest; adamant means unbreakable metal, here used for the helmets.
Ruth means pity or compassion, so 'neither ruth nor rest' means no mercy and no pause.
Drave is an old past tense of 'drove'; 'shore atwain' means cut in two.
'Leapt through the wounds the life' is inverted word order: life leapt out through the wounds.
The 'Trito-born' is Athena (Minerva), said to be born by Lake Tritonis or Triton's water. She inspires Meges here.
Niobe boasted of her many children, lost them to the gods, and was turned to stone on Sipylus, which still seemed to weep.
Niobe, whose children were slain by Apollo and Artemis for her boasting, wept until turned to stone on Mount Sipylus; the rock was said to seem to weep.
"Dreeing her weird" is archaic Scots: enduring her fate or doom.
Tydeus' son is Diomedes; Aeacus' scion is Achilles, grandson of Aeacus, though Achilles is absent from the fighting.
The "Goat-horned Star" is Capricorn, the winter sign; the simile evokes a winter sea storm at the solstice.
Enyo is a goddess of war; Eris is Strife; the Child of Leto is Artemis, the huntress.
"I trow" means "I believe"; "aweless" means fearless.
"Fill the measure up" means to complete the full quota of suffering destined for the Greeks before the god allows relief.
Aeaeus' son is Achilles, here named through his ancestor Aeacus; Penthesileia is fated to die by his hand.
The Maid is Penthesilea, queen of the Amazons, who has come to fight for Troy; the women watch her from the walls.
"Waxed" means grew; "lust of fight" means eager desire for battle, not sensual lust.
"Niggardly" means stingily; she asks whether God gave women less than men.
"Haled" means dragged by force; she fears enslavement after Troy falls.
"Infatuate" means foolishly carried away; Theano rebukes the women's rash enthusiasm.
"Danaan" means Greek; the Danaans are one of the names for the Greeks besieging Troy.
The Lord of War is Mars (Ares), reputed father of Penthesilea; this is only rumour in Theano's speech.
"Brake" is the archaic past tense of "broke"; "quailed" means shrank back in fear.
"Battle-bider" is a compound epithet meaning one who stands firm in battle.
Their fathers sailed with Hercules against Troy when Laomedon was king, and sacked it. Aias and Achilles recall that earlier conquest.
Atrytone is an epithet of Athena (Minerva in some translations), meaning the unwearied one.
The Aloeus' sons (the Aloadae, Otus and Ephialtes) tried to pile Ossa and Pelion upon Olympus to attack the gods.
The Fire-god is Hephaestus, who forged Achilles' divine armour.
"Recked" means heeded or cared about.
Xanthus is the river of Troy, into which Achilles had thrust many slain Trojans.
Chiron was the wise centaur who trained Achilles; his ash spear was a famous heirloom.
"Cozened" means tricked or deceived; Achilles asks who beguiled her into facing him.
"Guerdon" is an archaic word for a reward or payment.
"The works of women" refers to weaving and household tasks, which Achilles says she should have stayed with instead of war.
Aphrodite is called the Bride of the War-god, Ares, her lover in myth. Her making Penthesileia beautiful in death pierces Achilles with love.
"Levin-bolts" are lightning bolts; "welkin" is an old word for the sky.
"Reck not" means to pay no heed to or care nothing for.
The Titans were older gods who rebelled against Zeus and were imprisoned in Tartarus, the gloom beneath the earth.
The Amazon is Penthesilea, the warrior queen who has just fallen fighting for Troy; Achilles grieves over her body.
"Battle-blencher" means one who flinches from battle, a coward; Thersites turns the charge of weakness back on Achilles.
"Niddering" is an archaic word for a coward or base wretch.
Ate is the goddess of reckless folly and ruin, who leads people into blind error and then punishment.
Refers to an earlier occasion when Thersites abused Odysseus and escaped unharmed, as in the Iliad, where Odysseus beat him.
"Beard" means to confront or defy boldly to the face.
Diomedes, son of Tydeus, is Thersites' kinsman through Agrius, Thersites' father; hence his anger at the killing.
Atreid kings: Agamemnon and Menelaus, sons of Atreus. Later called "Atreus' sons".
Burg is an archaic word for a fortified town; the "burg of Ilus" is Troy, named for its founder Ilus.
"Boon" means a favour or request.
Quenching the pyre with wine was a funeral rite: the fire was put out after the body was burned.
Protesilaus was the first Greek to leap ashore at Troy and die, killed by Hector. Podarces was his brother.
"Niddering" is an archaic word for cowardly or base. "Corse" means corpse.
"Aeacus' son" is Achilles, whose father was Peleus, son of Aeacus. The Greeks acclaim him as victor.
"Peleus' son" is Achilles again. The poet uses patronymics in place of his name.

context_notes.text: Penthesileia, an Amazon queen and daughter of Ares, comes to aid Troy after Hector's death, seeking purification for killing her sister.
Twelve named companions follow her; the list that follows gives their names, and they are her handmaids as well as princes of war.
Priam, king of Troy, has lost many sons, including Hector, which explains his joyful welcome of a new champion.
Andromache was Hector's widow. Her father Eetion, king of Thebe, was killed by Achilles, who also killed her brothers.
Penthesileia, queen of the Amazons, has come to Troy as an ally after Hector's death, and Priam hosts her.
Pallas (Athena) favored the Greeks and so sends the deceptive dream to push Penthesileia into a fatal fight.
Penthesileia, queen of the Amazons, is the daughter of Ares, the War-god, who is the source of her armour.
Eris is the goddess of strife; she is closely associated with Ares and battle.
Zeus of Ida refers to Zeus worshipped on Mount Ida near Troy; Ilium is another name for Troy.
Dardanus was the ancestor of the Trojan royal line, so "Dardanus' blood" means the Trojan people.
Hector, Troy's great champion, has been killed by Achilles, so the Trojans had lost heart until the Amazons arrived.
Protesilaus of Phylace was the first Greek killed at Troy, so his men have long been fighting without him.
Oileus' son is the lesser Ajax; Tydeus' son is Diomedes. Both are Greek heroes.
The Maeander, in Asia Minor, gave English the word 'meander' for its winding course.
Penthesileia is queen of the Amazons, daughter of Ares, who has come to help Troy after Hector's death.
Menoetius' son is Patroclus, whose death Achilles and Aias (Ajax) still mourn at his tomb.
Ares is the god of war and Penthesileia's father.
Tisiphone is a Trojan woman, daughter of Antimachus. Antimachus was a Trojan elder, so she is of noble family.
Wool-working with distaff and loom was the standard work of women in the ancient world, so dropping it marks a break from their role.
Theano is a Trojan woman, wife of Antenor and priestess of Athena in Homer. Here she is a respected older voice of caution.
Penthesileia claims the war-god (Ares) as her father; in legend she was his daughter, queen of the Amazons, who came to aid Troy.
Aias (Ajax) was nearly invulnerable in legend, so Penthesileia's spear cannot wound him.
Achilles claims descent from Zeus (Cronos' Son) through his grandfather Aeacus.
Penthesileia is queen of the Amazons, a warrior people. She came to help Troy and was Ares' daughter.
Artemis is the virgin goddess of the hunt, often shown chasing game in the hills with her arrows.
Phthia was Achilles' homeland in Thessaly, where his father Peleus ruled.
Mount Ida overlooks Troy and served as a vantage point for the gods watching the war.
Achilles loved Penthesilea at the sight of her dying; Patroclus was his closest friend, killed by Hector at Troy.
Thersites is the ugly, abusive commoner among the Greeks, known from the Iliad for railing at leaders.
This alludes to Paris's passion for Helen, which caused the Trojan War.
Achilles is called son of Aeacus here, meaning grandson; Aeacus was Peleus' father.
Laomedon was an early king of Troy and Priam's father. His tomb was by the walls.
The Fire-god is Hephaestus, whose name stands for fire itself.
The Amazons were a warrior people of women who came to Troy as allies under Penthesileia.
Thersites was a Greek whom Achilles killed after he mocked Achilles over Penthesileia. So he is denied an honoured tomb.

literary_notes.text: The frightened Trojans are compared to cattle cowering in thickets from a lion, making Achilles a predator and Troy helpless prey.
Grief 'hovered dark-winged' over the Trojans like a bird of ill omen, making their dread almost physical.
Penthesileia outshining her companions is likened to the moon dominating the stars in a calm sky.
The Trojans' gladness is compared to farmers seeing a rainbow that promises rain, underlining how much they needed hope.
Priam's partial joy is compared to a half-healed blind man glimpsing light, conveying relief that still carries pain.
The narrator's exclamation tells us Penthesileia's boast is doomed, since Achilles is far stronger, foreshadowing her death.
Fate and death are pictured as figures standing close beside Penthesileia, making her doom feel immediate.
"Slain, Slain" repeats the word to stress Hector's fall and the grief it brought Troy.
The narrator steps back to offer a general reflection on faithful wives, turning Andromache's sorrow into a universal truth.
Daylight "dying" and the sun sinking mark the passing of time and quietly suggest coming death.
Sleep is compared to mist and to sweet dew, making the coming dream seem gentle and harmless.
The narrator calls her a fool for trusting the dream; the reader knows it is false while she exults.
The shield's rim is compared to the crescent moon rising over Ocean, giving the armour a cosmic, radiant grandeur.
Penthesileia in flaming armour is likened to Zeus's lightning, suggesting her terrifying power.
The words "first... and last" announce that this first battle will be her only one and that she will die.
The Trojans following her like sheep behind a ram suggests their trust and their unwitting path to slaughter.
The eagle seizing the dove symbolizes Penthesileia, or Troy's hopes, being overcome by a stronger power.
Priam's fear is confirmed by the narrator, whose knowledge of the Fates contrasts with the hopeful prayer just heard.
The Trojans are compared to ravening beasts, and Penthesileia to a wind-driven wildfire, stressing her destructive speed.
Rage is a cloak the Greeks put on, showing fury as armour they wear.
Bremusa's fall is likened to a felled pine, turning her death into a heavy, mournful image.
The slain women fall like calves under the butcher's axe, stressing helplessness and brutality.
The lion leaping on a flock makes the attacker predatory and the enemy frightened prey.
The mountain bows weeping and the crests echo the cry, giving nature human grief.
The weeping rock introduces a comparison of grief turned to stone, setting a tragic tone before the battle begins.
Onset-shout, Death, the Fates and Fearful Faces walk as figures on the battlefield, making war a living force.
Penthesileia is likened to a lioness attacking cattle, stressing her predatory ferocity and the Greeks' helplessness.
The storm-driven ship and crashing waves convey the Greek flight and the overwhelming pressure of her pursuit.
Falling Greeks are compared to autumn leaves and raindrops, emphasizing their number and the inevitability of death.
The narrator reveals the boasting Trojan's coming doom, which he cannot foresee.
Doom lights her path with glory toward death, hinting at her coming defeat by Achilles.
Tisiphone argues for equality by listing shared eyes, limbs, air and food, building her case through repetition.
Bondage looms as a "fearful shadow", making the threat of slavery a dark presence behind the women's grief.
The women stirring to arms are compared to bees leaving the hive in spring, showing their shared restless eagerness.
Theano is shown as wise and persuasive, her age and experience giving her authority that calms the crowd.
The Achaeans slaughtered by Penthesileia are compared to goats torn by a panther, stressing their helplessness.
A storm uprooting and snapping forest trees pictures the Greek army felled by Penthesileia's spear.
Aias and Achilles are likened to two lions among sheep, showing their predatory power.
Penthesileia is compared to a leaping leopard facing hunters, making her fierce yet doomed.
Achilles' taunt that her hour "is come" proves true immediately, as his spear kills her.
The spear piercing horse and rider is compared to meat on a spit, a homely, brutal image.
Her fall is compared to a tall pine snapped by Boreas, linking her beauty and pathos with nature.
The fleeing Trojans are likened to shipwreck survivors mourning lost shipmates, turning flight into grief.
Her face rising into view is compared to the breaking dawn, which makes her beauty seem radiant and her death a loss.
Love is imagined as a sharp arrow piercing Achilles, which ties his sudden remorse to Aphrodite's power.
Achilles mocked her moments ago, yet now he longs to have made her his bride, a reversal he caused himself.
Ares' descent is likened to Zeus's thunderbolt, an image that conveys speed, brightness and menace.
A boulder rolling down a mountain until the plain stops it mirrors Ares' furious rush halted by Zeus.
Thersites sneers that Achilles lusts after an Amazon as if she were a modest bride, mocking the warrior queen's nature.
His moralizing about lust and ruin recalls Troy's fall through Helen, making his taunt sound righteous even though he is a bitter, spiteful speaker.
The vivid violence of one blow shattering teeth and driving out the soul shows Achilles' overwhelming strength.
Justice and Ate are pictured as living powers who watch and punish arrogant speech.
"Unkennels thy dog's soul" pictures Thersites' spirit as a cur driven from its kennel, expressing contempt.
Fire is called a god with "swift-upleaping might" and "ravening" appetite, as if it were a living beast devouring the body.
The Trojans' grief is compared to that for a beloved daughter. It shows how deeply they honour the foreign queen.
The narrator states a general truth about mercy toward dead enemies, giving moral weight to the Greeks' generosity.
The deaths of two brothers are paired, Protesilaus by Hector and Podarces by Penthesileia. The echo makes the Greek loss feel doomed and repeated.
Thersites is thrown into a separate pit and called wretched, in sharp contrast with the high mound of Podarces.
